---
title: "what is mlops?"
---

## the idea

- mlops, short for machine learning operations, is the practice of developing, releasing, and operating ml systems reliably
- a model is a learned mapping from inputs to predictions; deployment makes that model available in a working system, while serving runs it on new inputs
- training produces a model; a usable system also needs repeatable data processing, evaluation, serving, and monitoring
- software engineering supplies maintainable code and tests; devops supplies release and infrastructure practices; mlops extends these to changing data and learned models [aws overview](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/mlops/)

## why a good model is not enough

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| problem | practice that helps |
|---|---|
| “which data produced this model?” | record data, code, configuration, and model versions |
| “it worked in my notebook” | package dependencies and use a repeatable entry point |
| “training and prediction disagree” | save preprocessing with the model |
| “a new release broke predictions” | test releases and keep a rollback path |
| “performance changed after release” | monitor inputs, outcomes, and service health |

:::

- reproducibility means being able to trace and rerun an experiment; a seed alone does not capture its data or environment
- scikit-learn is a python library for preprocessing, modelling, and evaluation; use its pipeline to bundle preprocessing with an estimator, the component that learns from data [pipeline documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html)

## a few working terms

- dependencies are the libraries and software a program needs; record their versions to recreate its environment
- an artifact is a saved output such as a fitted model or prediction file; keep it when another step needs the result
- an orchestrator coordinates tasks and their dependencies; use one when several processing steps must run in a defined order
- rollback restores a previous working version; plan it before releasing a replacement
- monitoring observes system behaviour over time; drift means data distributions or input–outcome relationships have changed, which may require investigation

## three kinds of automation

- **ci: continuous integration:** automatically check changes to code, data interfaces, and model behaviour
- **cd: continuous delivery/deployment:** prepare a validated release; continuous delivery can retain a manual approval, while continuous deployment automates release
- **ct: continuous training:** retrain on a trigger such as new data or a schedule, then validate the candidate before promotion
- google describes a progression from manual workflows, to automated ml pipelines, to ci/cd for those pipelines [google’s mlops guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning)

## implement the smallest useful version

- start with one dataset, one baseline, and a script that trains and evaluates a pipeline
- record the dataset version, code commit, parameters, metrics, and dependencies with the saved model
- add a reload-and-predict check; then automate checks when code changes
- introduce a [registry](../experiments/registry.qmd) to catalogue model versions, or a [feature store](../data-pipelines/versioning.qmd) to organise reusable features, when the workflow needs them
- mlflow is an experiment-tracking and model-management tool; use it to organise runs, compare metrics, and retrieve saved artifacts [mlflow quickstart](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/tracking/quickstart/)
